column2: Which statement is an observation?

column2: Which term means a conclusion built from observations and evidence?
column4: inference

column2: Which term is a proposed explanation or prediction that can be tested?
column4: measurement

column2: Which term describes a broad explanation supported by a large body of well-tested information?
column4: measurement

column2: Which term describes a simplified representation used to explain or predict a physical situation?
column4: law

column2: A student records that a shadow is 12 cm long and concludes the light source is not directly overhead. Which part is the inference?
column4: The light source is not directly overhead.

column2: Why can a simplified model still be scientifically useful?
column4: It guarantees every prediction will be correct.
column5: It can preserve the relationships important to the question even if some details are omitted.
column6: It removes the need for measurements.

column2: Which claim is most testable?
column3: A hidden cause changes motion but can never be detected.
column4: Nature prefers this result.
column5: The result occurs for an unknowable reason.
column6: A cart released from a higher ramp position travels farther on the same floor.

column2: Repeated measurements disagree with a model’s prediction. What is the best response?
column3: Check the measurements and assumptions, then revise the model if the disagreement remains.
column4: Ignore the measurements.
column5: Keep the model unchanged because it came first.
column6: Change the data to fit the model.

column2: Why should a student identify what each symbol in a formula represents before calculating?
column3: To make the calculator work faster.
column4: To connect the mathematical relationship to the measured physical quantities and assumptions.
column5: To guarantee the measurements are exact.

column2: A precise calculation is based on a poorly estimated distance. Which evaluation is strongest?
column3: The answer must be correct because the arithmetic is precise.
column4: The estimate becomes exact inside a formula.
column5: The result may not be well supported because the input evidence is weak.
column6: Only the number of decimal places matters.

column2: Model A is visually realistic but fails to predict new measurements. Model B is simpler but correctly predicts them. Which evaluation is best?
column3: Model A is better because it has more detail.
column4: Both models are equally strong because all models are simplified.
column5: Neither model can be evaluated with evidence.
column6: Model B is more useful for this question because its preserved relationship fits the evidence.

column2: Which choice is an inference rather than an observation?
column3: The spacing in the photo suggests the object is speeding up.
column4: The timer reads 3.8 s.

column2: Which pair correctly matches the terms?
column4: Observation—directly recorded; inference—conclusion built from evidence.

column2: Why must a scientific claim be testable?
column3: So it will always be true.
column4: So it never needs revision.
column5: So evidence could support or challenge it.
column6: So authority can decide the result.

column2: Which result would provide the strongest challenge to a claim?
column4: The claim uses a short equation.
column6: A careful repeatable measurement that contradicts its prediction.

column2: A model predicts equal ratios in repeated trials. Which evidence best supports it?
column3: Several independent trials give nearly the same expected ratio.
column4: One trial gives the expected ratio.
column6: The model was made by an expert.

column2: Which action best evaluates whether an explanation is supported?
column3: Count how many scientific words it uses.
column4: Compare its predictions with observations and measurements.

column2: Which statement best describes a formula in physics?
column4: A guarantee that assumptions are correct.
column5: A compact model showing how quantities relate.
column6: A rule that makes estimates exact.

column2: A formula gives a result that conflicts with careful measurements. What should a physicist do first?
column3: Keep the formula result because equations cannot be wrong.
column4: Discard the measurements without checking them.
column5: Add more decimal places to the calculation.
column6: Check the measurements, assumptions, and whether the formula applies to the situation.
